title: Space Stations and the Space Shuttle
summary: After the Moon, people wanted to LIVE in space, so they built houses in orbit called space stations. Then America built the Space Shuttle, a spaceship with wings that landed on a runway like a giant glider and flew again and again. It launched telescopes, carried the first American women and Black astronauts to space, and taught us hard lessons about safety.

sections.heading: A House in the Sky: Salyut 1
paragraphs: Landing on the Moon was like a sprint: a few days there, a few days back, splashdown, parade. But scientists knew that if humans were ever going to explore the solar system properly, they needed to learn something much harder. They needed to learn how to live in space for weeks and months. How do you sleep, eat, wash, work and stay healthy when everything floats? The only way to find out was to build a home in orbit. That home is called a space station: a spacecraft big enough to live in, which stays in orbit for years while crews come and go.

The Soviet Union got there first. On 19 April 1971 a powerful Proton rocket roared away from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan carrying Salyut 1, the world's first space station. Salyut means 'salute' or 'fireworks' in Russian. The launch had been planned for 12 April, exactly ten years after Yuri Gagarin's flight, but technical problems delayed it by a week. Salyut 1 was a metal tube about 16 metres long, longer than a city bus, weighing around 18 tonnes. It had solar panels sticking out like wings, a docking port at one end, and inside there was room for a small crew, scientific instruments and even a telescope.

The first crew to try to move in had bad luck. In April 1971 the Soyuz 10 spacecraft reached the station and touched its docking port, but the latches would not lock tightly. The cosmonauts could not open the hatch, so after a few hours they had to fly home without ever going inside. Engineers worked fast, and in June the next crew set off on Soyuz 11: Georgy Dobrovolsky, the commander, Vladislav Volkov and Viktor Patsayev. On 7 June 1971 they docked successfully, opened the hatch, and floated into the first house in space.

Then came the tragedy. Late on 29 June 1971 the three men climbed back into their Soyuz, undocked and began the trip home. As the spacecraft separated into its parts before re-entry, a small valve that was supposed to stay shut until much later was jolted open. Air rushed out of the cabin into the vacuum of space in less than a minute. The cosmonauts were not wearing spacesuits, because the cabin was too small to fit three people in suits, and there was no way to close the valve in time. When the capsule landed gently on its parachute in Kazakhstan and the recovery team opened the hatch, they found that all three men had died. They are still the only people known to have died above the Kármán line, in space itself.

Afterwards, Soviet engineers made a firm rule: cosmonauts must wear pressure suits during launch and landing. Salyut 1 itself was steered into the Pacific Ocean on 11 October 1971, after about 175 days in orbit, and more Salyut stations followed.

sections.heading: Skylab: A Workshop Made from a Moon Rocket
paragraphs: America's first space station had a clever origin. When the last Apollo Moon missions were cancelled, NASA had spare Saturn V rockets. Engineers took the empty third stage of one of them, the giant fuel tank called the S-IVB, and turned it into a home. Instead of filling it with liquid hydrogen, they filled it with sleeping cabins, a kitchen table, a shower, an exercise bike, cupboards of food and a whole observatory for studying the Sun. They called it Skylab.

Skylab was launched on 14 May 1973 on the very last Saturn V ever to fly. It was huge for its time, about 25 metres long and weighing around 77 tonnes, with roughly as much living space as a small house. But the launch went badly wrong. About a minute after liftoff, a thin metal shield designed to protect the station from tiny space rocks and the heat of the Sun was torn away by the rushing air. It ripped off one of the two big solar panel wings and jammed the other one shut. Once in orbit, Skylab had very little electrical power, and without its shield the inside started to bake in the sunlight, with temperatures reportedly climbing above 50 degrees Celsius.

The first crew, Pete Conrad, Joseph Kerwin and Paul Weitz, launched on 25 May 1973 with a new job: rescue the station. They had brought a folding sunshade that worked like a giant umbrella. They pushed it out through a small airlock in the side of Skylab and opened it over the hot outer wall. Slowly, the temperature inside fell to a comfortable level. Then, on a daring spacewalk, Conrad and Kerwin used cutting tools and a long pole to free the jammed solar wing. When it finally swung open, power flowed into the station again. It was the first time astronauts had repaired a crippled spacecraft in orbit, and it showed how valuable human hands and brains could be in space.

Over the next nine months three crews lived aboard Skylab. The second crew stayed 59 and a half days and the third crew, from 16 November 1973 to 8 February 1974, stayed 84 days, a record that would last for years. Skylab's crews took tens of thousands of photographs of the Sun with the station's special telescopes, capturing huge solar flares and loops of glowing gas. They photographed Earth's forests, crops and storms, and studied what long stays in weightlessness do to the heart, muscles and bones.

After the last crew left, NASA hoped that a Space Shuttle might one day boost Skylab higher. But the Shuttle was not ready in time, and the thin upper air slowly dragged the station down. On 11 July 1979 Skylab re-entered the atmosphere. Most of it burned up, but some pieces fell into the Indian Ocean and scattered across a remote, thinly populated part of Western Australia. Nobody was hurt, and some fragments ended up in museums.

sections.heading: From a Handshake to Mir
paragraphs: For almost twenty years the space race had been a contest between rivals. But in the early 1970s the leaders of the United States and the Soviet Union agreed to try a joint mission, the Apollo–Soyuz Test Project. There was a practical problem: the two spacecraft had different docking systems and even different air inside. Apollo used pure oxygen at low pressure, while Soyuz used an Earth-like air mix, and switching too fast could give astronauts the 'bends', the painful illness divers get when pressure changes quickly. So the Americans built a special docking module, a short tube that worked as an adapter and an airlock at the same time.

On 15 July 1975 both spacecraft launched on the same day, Soyuz 19 from Baikonur and, about seven and a half hours later, the last Apollo spacecraft ever flown from Florida. The Soviet crew was Alexei Leonov, the cosmonaut who had made the first spacewalk, and engineer Valery Kubasov. The American crew was Thomas Stafford, Vance Brand and Deke Slayton, one of the original Mercury Seven astronauts who had finally made it to space after years grounded by a heart problem.

On 17 July 1975 the two ships docked. A few hours later Stafford and Leonov reached through the open hatch and shook hands, while television viewers around the world watched. The crews visited each other's spacecraft, shared meals, swapped gifts, and practised each other's languages: the Americans spoke Russian and the Soviets spoke English, which made for some funny moments. They stayed linked together for about two days before going their separate ways.

Meanwhile the Soviets kept improving their Salyut stations. Salyut 6, launched in 1977, and Salyut 7, launched in 1982, had two docking ports instead of one. That meant robot cargo ships called Progress, first flown in 1978, could deliver food, water, air, fuel and mail while a crew stayed aboard, so crews could now live in orbit for half a year or more. Visitors came too, including Vladimír Remek of Czechoslovakia in 1978, the first person in space from a country other than the USSR or the USA, and in 1984 Rakesh Sharma, the first Indian in space.

On 20 February 1986 the Soviet Union launched the core of a new kind of space station. It was called Mir, a Russian word that can mean both 'peace' and 'world'. The core module looked a lot like a Salyut, but with one big difference: at its front end was a ball-shaped docking hub with several ports. Mir was designed to grow. Over the next ten years, new modules were launched one by one and attached to the hub, like rooms being added to a house. A small docking module was carried up by an American Space Shuttle in 1995. Mir became the first truly modular space station, with seven pressurised modules, and it weighed about 130 tonnes when it was complete.

Mir was also the place where people pushed the limits of the human body. The doctor-cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov lived aboard for 437 days in a row in 1994 and 1995, carefully studying what happened to his own heart, muscles and mind. It is still the longest single spaceflight by any human. When he came back to Earth, he insisted on walking the few steps from the capsule to a chair by himself, to show that people could survive a trip as long as a journey to Mars.

Between 1994 and 1998 the United States and Russia ran the Shuttle–Mir program. American Space Shuttles flew eleven missions linked to Mir, docking with it nine times, and seven American astronauts lived aboard for months, side by side with Russian crewmates. The first docking, by the Shuttle Atlantis in June 1995, joined two of the biggest spacecraft ever built into a single giant ship. These flights let both countries learn to work together in orbit before building something much bigger.

By 2000 Mir was old, and Russia needed its money and attention for the new International Space Station. On 23 March 2001, after 15 years in orbit, mission controllers fired the engines of a docked Progress ship to slow Mir down. The great station broke apart and burned in the sky over the South Pacific, with the surviving pieces splashing harmlessly into the ocean far from land.

sections.heading: A Spaceship with Wings
paragraphs: While the Soviets built stations, NASA wanted a spaceship that could fly to orbit, land on a runway and fly again a few weeks later, instead of throwing away a whole rocket every time. It was called the Space Shuttle.

The Shuttle had three main parts, and you could recognise them from far away. The first was the orbiter, the white winged spaceship with a black belly that looked like a stubby aeroplane. It was about 37 metres long, with a wingspan of about 24 metres, and it carried the crew, usually seven people, plus a cargo hold called the payload bay, 18 metres long and 4.6 metres wide, big enough to carry a bus. At its tail were three main engines that burned liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen.

Those engines did not carry their own fuel. It came from the second part, the huge orange external tank, about 47 metres tall, which the orbiter rode on like a rider on a horse. Inside were two separate tanks, a big one for liquid hydrogen and a smaller one for liquid oxygen, kept at hundreds of degrees below zero. The third part was a pair of tall, thin solid rocket boosters strapped to the sides of the tank. Each was about 45 metres tall. Like giant fireworks, they burned a rubbery solid propellant and provided most of the push at liftoff, well over two-thirds of the thrust.

A launch went like this. The main engines lit a few seconds before liftoff, then the boosters ignited and the whole stack leapt off the pad. About two minutes later, the empty boosters dropped away and floated down to the Atlantic Ocean on parachutes, where ships picked them up so they could be cleaned and refilled. About eight and a half minutes after liftoff, the main engines shut down and the external tank was dropped. It was the only part not reused; it fell back and broke up over a remote part of the ocean.

Coming home was the most unusual part. The orbiter fired small engines to slow down, then dropped into the atmosphere belly-first. About 24,000 heat-resistant tiles, made mostly of a light silica foam, protected the underside. The nose and the front edges of the wings, the hottest parts, were covered with a tough grey material called reinforced carbon-carbon. After re-entry, the orbiter had no working engines at all. It was a glider, a very heavy one, and the commander had exactly one chance to line up with the runway. It touched down at more than 300 kilometres per hour and used a parachute to help it stop.

The first Shuttle flight launched on 12 April 1981, exactly 20 years after Yuri Gagarin's flight. The orbiter was Columbia, and the crew was just two people: commander John Young, a veteran who had walked on the Moon on Apollo 16, and pilot Robert Crippen. It was the first time NASA had ever put people aboard a new kind of rocket on its very first flight, with no uncrewed test first. After 37 orbits in just over two days, Columbia glided down onto a dry lake bed at Edwards Air Force Base in California on 14 April. Thousands of people cheered as the spaceship rolled to a stop.

Five orbiters flew in space: Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, Atlantis and Endeavour, which was built later to replace Challenger. A test orbiter called Enterprise, named after the starship in Star Trek after fans wrote in, never reached space but made gliding tests in 1977.

sections.heading: New Faces in Space
paragraphs: In 1978 NASA chose a new group of astronauts that, for the first time, included women and people of colour. One of them was Sally Ride, a physicist from California who had also been a talented tennis player. On 18 June 1983 she launched aboard Challenger on mission STS-7 and became the first American woman in space. She was 32, and she operated the Shuttle's robotic arm, a long jointed arm built in Canada and nicknamed Canadarm, to release a satellite and grab it again.

Just two months later, on 30 August 1983, Challenger launched again on STS-8, this time at night, the first night launch of the Shuttle program. Aboard was Guion Bluford, an engineer and air force fighter pilot from Philadelphia who had flown 144 combat missions. He became the first African American in space. Bluford went on to fly four Shuttle missions in total.

On 12 September 1992, the orbiter Endeavour lifted off with Mae Jemison aboard. Jemison was a doctor, an engineer and a dancer who had worked as a medical officer in the Peace Corps in West Africa. She became the first African American woman in space. On her mission she studied, among other things, how frogs' eggs developed in weightlessness, and, as a big Star Trek fan, she opened her work shifts with the famous line 'Hailing frequencies open'. The same flight carried Mamoru Mohri, the first Japanese astronaut to fly on a Shuttle.

sections.heading: Fixing Hubble's Blurry Eye
paragraphs: Above the air, starlight is not blurred by the wobbling atmosphere that makes stars twinkle. That is why astronomers had dreamed for decades of a big telescope in orbit. On 24 April 1990 the Shuttle Discovery carried the Hubble Space Telescope into space, and the next day astronauts released it from the robotic arm. Hubble is about the size of a school bus, roughly 13 metres long, and its main mirror is 2.4 metres across. It is named after Edwin Hubble, the astronomer who showed in the 1920s that the universe is full of galaxies and is expanding.

But when the first pictures came back, astronomers' hearts sank. The images were fuzzy. Engineers discovered that the main mirror had been ground to slightly the wrong shape. The mistake was tiny, about 2 micrometres at the edges, about one fiftieth of the thickness of a human hair, but for a precision telescope it was enough to smear the light. This kind of flaw is called spherical aberration.

Here the Shuttle showed what it could do that no throwaway rocket could. Hubble had been designed so that astronauts could visit and swap its parts. In December 1993 the Shuttle Endeavour flew the first servicing mission, STS-61. Over five spacewalks lasting more than 35 hours in total, astronauts installed a new camera called the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2, whose optics contained a correction for the mirror's flaw, rather like a prescription for glasses. They also added a box of small corrective mirrors called COSTAR to fix the light going to the other instruments, and they replaced the solar panels and gyroscopes.

In January 1994 the first new images arrived, and they were sharp and stunning. Hubble went on to become one of the most productive scientific instruments in history. It helped measure how fast the universe is expanding, photographed galaxies more than ten billion light-years away, and watched comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 crash into Jupiter in 1994. Shuttle crews visited Hubble five times in all, the last in 2009, each time leaving it better than before. Hubble is still working today, more than 35 years after launch.

sections.heading: Two Sad Days
paragraphs: The first was 28 January 1986. Challenger was ready to launch on mission STS-51-L from Florida. Aboard were commander Dick Scobee, pilot Michael Smith, mission specialists Ronald McNair, Ellison Onizuka and Judith Resnik, engineer Gregory Jarvis, and Christa McAuliffe, a high school teacher from New Hampshire. McAuliffe had been chosen from more than 11,000 applicants to be the first teacher in space, and she planned to teach lessons to schoolchildren from orbit. Because of her, millions of students were watching on television in their classrooms.

The morning was unusually cold for Florida, about 2 degrees Celsius, and icicles hung from the launch tower. Each solid rocket booster was built in segments, and the joints between them were sealed with rubber rings called O-rings. Engineers from the company that made the boosters had worried that cold rubber becomes stiff and might not seal properly. They had argued the night before that the launch should wait for warmer weather, but managers decided to go ahead.

At 11:38 in the morning Challenger lifted off. Hidden from view, hot gas began leaking through a joint on the right booster, like a blowtorch. About 73 seconds into the flight, the flame weakened the external tank and the structure holding it, the tank came apart, and the orbiter was torn apart by the enormous forces of the air rushing past at nearly twice the speed of sound. A huge cloud appeared in the sky. All seven astronauts were lost.

A special group called the Rogers Commission investigated. One of its members, the famous physicist Richard Feynman, showed the problem in the simplest possible way on live television: he squeezed a piece of O-ring rubber in a clamp, dipped it in a glass of ice-cold water, and showed that it did not spring back. The commission also found that NASA's decision-making had not listened properly to the engineers' warnings. The Shuttle was grounded for almost three years while the boosters were redesigned, and it returned to flight with Discovery in September 1988.

The second sad day was 1 February 2003. Columbia, the first orbiter ever to fly, was coming home from a 16-day science mission, STS-107, with more than 80 experiments aboard. Its crew was commander Rick Husband, pilot William McCool, Michael Anderson, David Brown, Laurel Clark, Kalpana Chawla and Ilan Ramon. Chawla had been born in Karnal, India, and was the first woman of Indian birth to fly in space. Ramon was the first astronaut from Israel. Just over 81 seconds after launch, on 16 January, a briefcase-sized piece of hard foam insulation had broken off the external tank and struck the front edge of Columbia's left wing. Nobody on the ground realised how badly it had damaged the wing's protective carbon panels.

When Columbia re-entered the atmosphere, superheated air poured in through the hole in the wing and slowly melted the structure inside. Over Texas, only about 16 minutes before landing, the orbiter broke apart. All seven astronauts were lost. Investigators found that foam had hit the Shuttle on earlier flights too, and that it had come to be treated as a normal nuisance instead of a serious danger.

After Columbia, every Shuttle carried a long boom with cameras and lasers so astronauts could inspect the heat shield in orbit, and the crews practised repair techniques. The 14 astronauts lost on Challenger and Columbia are remembered with memorials, schools, craters on the Moon and even asteroids named after them. Their loss changed how NASA thinks about safety, especially the importance of listening when engineers say something is wrong.

sections.heading: Buran, the Last Landing and What Came Next
paragraphs: The Soviet Union worried that the American Shuttle might give the United States a military advantage, so it built its own. It was called Buran, which means 'snowstorm', and from the outside it looked so much like the American orbiter that people sometimes mixed up photographs. But there were important differences. Buran had no big main engines of its own. Instead, it rode on the side of a gigantic rocket called Energia, whose own engines and strap-on boosters did all the work of reaching orbit. That meant Energia could also launch other heavy cargo without an orbiter at all.

On 15 November 1988 Buran launched from Baikonur with nobody aboard. It circled Earth twice, re-entered and then, completely under computer control, glided down and landed on a runway at Baikonur, close to its target, in strong crosswinds. It was the first spaceplane ever to fly to orbit and land fully automatically. It was an impressive success. But it was also Buran's only flight. The Soviet Union was running out of money, and after the country broke apart in 1991 there were no funds to continue. The program was cancelled in 1993. Sadly, in 2002 the roof of the hangar where the flown Buran was stored at Baikonur collapsed, destroying it.

The American Shuttle kept flying for another two decades. In its last years, its most important job was building the International Space Station, carrying up big modules, solar panels and trusses in its payload bay and using its robotic arm to fit them together. But after the loss of Columbia, the United States decided the Shuttle had become too old, too expensive and too risky. In 2004 it was announced that the Shuttle would retire once the space station was finished.

The last mission, STS-135, launched on 8 July 2011 with a crew of four: Chris Ferguson, Doug Hurley, Sandra Magnus and Rex Walheim. Atlantis delivered supplies to the space station and, on 21 July 2011, glided down to the runway at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida for the final time.

Altogether the Shuttle flew 135 missions over 30 years. It carried hundreds of astronauts, launched dozens of satellites and space probes, repaired Hubble, and helped build a space station. Today the surviving orbiters are museum pieces: Discovery is at the Smithsonian's Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center near Washington, D.C., Atlantis is at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, Endeavour is at the California Science Center in Los Angeles, and Enterprise is aboard the Intrepid Museum in New York. You can stand under them and look up at the scorched tiles on their bellies.

But the most important thing the Shuttle helped create is still flying right now, above your head. Former rivals who had once raced each other to the Moon had shaken hands in orbit, shared Mir, and learned to trust one another. Now they were ready to build together the biggest, most complicated and most expensive thing humans have ever put in space: a station that would never be empty.

deepDive: Why did the Shuttle, designed to make spaceflight cheap and routine, end up so costly? Historians usually point to compromises made in the early 1970s. NASA first sketched a fully reusable two-stage vehicle: a winged booster with a pilot that would fly back to the launch site, carrying a winged orbiter. Budgets were cut, and the Air Force, whose support NASA needed, demanded a large payload bay and the ability to glide sideways a long way during re-entry. The result was a partly reusable design: an orbiter with expensive, high-performance hydrogen engines, recoverable solid boosters that had to be fished out of the sea and rebuilt, and a throwaway tank. Early plans spoke of around 50 flights a year. In reality the busiest year, 1985, saw nine flights, and the program averaged about 4 to 5 a year. Each orbiter needed months of work on its roughly 24,000 tiles and its three main engines between flights. Counting all development and operations, the program cost on the order of 200 billion US dollars in today's money, which works out to well over a billion dollars per flight. Safety was the other hard lesson. The Shuttle had no launch escape system for most of its climb, and because the orbiter sat beside the tank instead of on top, falling debris such as foam could strike it. Both investigations, the Rogers Commission in 1986 and the Columbia Accident Investigation Board in 2003, concluded that the technical causes were made worse by organisational ones: schedule pressure and a habit of treating repeated small problems as acceptable. The sociologist Diane Vaughan called this the 'normalization of deviance'. Yet the Shuttle also did things no other vehicle could. It could carry about 27 tonnes into low orbit, brought satellites back down for repair, served as a laboratory, and lifted most of the large pieces of the International Space Station. Stations taught a complementary lesson: long-duration flights by Salyut, Skylab and Mir showed that bones and muscles weaken and fluids shift towards the head in weightlessness, but that exercise and careful medicine let people stay healthy for a year or more.
funFact: Valeri Polyakov's 437 days aboard Mir in 1994 and 1995 is still the longest single trip any human has made in space.
